questions.prompt: What does DNS do when you visit example.com?

options.text: It encrypts the connection to the server
It translates the name example.com into an IP address
It delivers the page content in order
It decides which server in a data centre handles the request

questions.explanation: DNS is the internet's directory: it maps names to IP addresses. Encryption is TLS's job, and reliable ordered delivery is TCP's.

questions.prompt: How many round trips does a TCP handshake cost before the client can send its request?
questions.explanation: The handshake has three messages (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), but the client can send data with the final ACK, so it waits for one full round trip.
questions.hint: Count how many times the client has to wait for an answer.

questions.prompt: A server answers 429 Too Many Requests. Which family is this, and whose side is the problem on?

options.text: 4xx: the client should change what it's doing (here, slow down)

questions.explanation: 4xx codes mean the request needs to change. 429 tells the client it's sending too fast and should back off, often guided by a Retry-After header.

questions.prompt: A server is 100 ms away (one round trip = 100 ms). Which changes reduce the time before the first byte of a page arrives? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reusing an existing connection with keep-alive
Serving the page from a CDN location 10 ms away
Doubling the server's CPU speed when the server takes 2 ms
Using TLS 1.3 instead of TLS 1.2 for new connections

questions.explanation: Keep-alive skips the TCP and TLS handshakes, a CDN shortens every round trip, and TLS 1.3 needs one handshake round trip instead of two. Halving 2 ms of server time saves only 1 ms out of hundreds.
questions.hint: Where is the time actually going: in round trips or on the server?

questions.prompt: Why does HTTP/3 avoid head-of-line blocking between requests on the same connection?

options.text: It sends each request over a separate TCP connection
It runs over QUIC, where each stream is delivered independently, so a lost packet only delays its own stream
It disables encryption so packets are smaller

questions.explanation: TCP delivers one ordered byte stream, so a lost packet stalls everything behind it. QUIC (on UDP) has independent streams, so loss on one doesn't block the others. It still encrypts everything with TLS 1.3.
